content.prompt: Calculate the mode, range, median, and mean. Round to 1 d.p. if required.

answer.worked:
Ordered data: $12,16,16,19,19,22,27,34,35$.

Both $16$ and $19$ occur twice, so the modes are $16$ and $19$. The fifth value is $19$, so the median is $19$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=35-12\\\text{Range}&=23\\\bar{x}&=\frac{19+34+22+16+27+35+19+12+16}{9}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{200}{9}\\\bar{x}&\approx22.2\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $23,38,42,42,52,54,65,68$.

$42$ occurs twice, so the mode is $42$. The middle values are $42$ and $52$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=68-23\\\text{Range}&=45\\\text{Median}&=\frac{42+52}{2}\\\text{Median}&=47\\\bar{x}&=\frac{68+54+23+42+38+52+65+42}{8}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{384}{8}\\\bar{x}&=48\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $205,205,240,240,256,296,310$.

Both $205$ and $240$ occur twice, so the modes are $205$ and $240$. The fourth value is $240$, so the median is $240$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=310-205\\\text{Range}&=105\\\bar{x}&=\frac{240+310+205+296+240+256+205}{7}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{1752}{7}\\\bar{x}&\approx250.3\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

Ordered data: $21,23,23,56,66,80,87$.

$23$ occurs twice, so the mode is $23$. The fourth value is $56$, so the median is $56$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Range}&=87-21\\\text{Range}&=66\\\bar{x}&=\frac{80+23+56+21+87+66+23}{7}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{356}{7}\\\bar{x}&\approx50.9\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: The mean doesn’t have to be part of the dataset, but a mode, when one exists, always is.

answer.short: A mode, when one exists, is a most frequent data value, so it belongs to the dataset. A mean need not: $0$ and $10$ have mean $5$.
answer.worked:
A mode is a value occurring most frequently in the dataset, so any mode must be a data value. For the data $0,10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\frac{0+10}{2}\\\bar{x}&=5\end{aligned}$$
Since $5$ is absent from the data, the mean need not be a data value. This example demonstrates the mean claim; it has no mode under the booklet’s convention.

children.prompt: Does the median always have to be a part of the dataset? Justify your answer.

answer.short: No. For $0,10$, the median is $\frac{0+10}{2}=5$, which is not a data value.
answer.worked:
With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. For the data $0,10$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Median}&=\frac{0+10}{2}\\\text{Median}&=5\end{aligned}$$
The value $5$ is not in the dataset, so the median need not be a data value. With an odd number of values, the median is the actual middle data value.
